Keep in mind that macroeconomics is difficult and mostly speculative. That's why I avoid the likes of Rubin, Reich, and Krugman. None of them allow for the idea that they are constructing a model from an insanely complex set of variables. As far as they're concerned, their word is fact incarnate.

Kling and Boudreaux, on the other hand, are more willing to allow for a margin of error- that they believe their model to be correct but that in macroeconomics you often don't know the effect of a change until you make the change and observe the effect.

A little Googling gets some of Kling's opinions- that the sky isn't falling, Greece leaving the Euro isn't a financial disaster, and that this issue may be more of a political one than an economic one. While I'm no expert, I've always found what I understand of Kling's writing to be well reasoned and well thought out. For what it's worth.
